title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Sandbox — Matt Brockman, E2B
talk_summary: A workshop-style talk from E2B about running agent code in fast-starting, snapshot/resume sandboxes, walking through failure modes (CPU/memory/disk exhaustion, orphan processes, sandbox lifecycle, user-to-sandbox mapping, filesystem permissions) via a capture-the-flag.

takeaways.technique: Snapshot/resume sandbox state instead of cold rebuilds
takeaways.numbers: aim to spin up sandboxes in less than 100ms

takeaways.technique: Two-phase sandbox lifetime (long while working, short after task)
takeaways.what_they_do: Give a sandbox a long command timeout while a task runs, then drop the lifetime to a short timeout once the task completes so idle sandboxes free resources.
Replace round-robin sandbox assignment with a persistent map (DB/dict) of user to sandbox ID so the same agent/user reuses its sandbox and can be audited historically.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of giving us a roundroin uh sandbox assignment we're going to keep track by user of what sandbox they get

takeaways.technique: Orphan process reaping as routine maintenance
takeaways.what_they_do: Because resumed sandboxes retain old processes, they periodically scan for and kill leaked child processes; orphan cleanup is treated as core sandbox management.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a lot of sandbox management ends up being killing orphans

takeaways.what_they_do: Separate read-only template cache from writable runtime cache and restrict which paths agents can write, rather than granting full filesystem access.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a lot of times you don't want your agents writing to every single part of your file system

takeaways.what_they_do: They teach operators to detect and remediate CPU pegging, memory blowups, and disk fills inside sandboxes, and to reset via snapshot reload when a sandbox is corrupted.
takeaways.evidence_quote: all these things have limited resources uh and all these things you're going to run into at some point
